opNames.toEmptyStack: conversion to acceptance by empty stack
opNames.toFinalState: conversion to acceptance by final state

error.operatorNeedsExpr: The "{{op}}" operator must be preceded by an expression (position {{pos}}).

build.title: Automaton from the expression
build.detail: The expression is built inside out: each subexpression's automaton is made from the automata of its parts. A letter a gets a single a-transition, ε a single accepting state, ∅ a single state that never accepts. r₁ + r₂: a new start state with ε-transitions into both start states, accepting where either one does. r₁r₂: ε-transitions from the first one's accepting states into the second one's start, accepting where the second one does. r*: a new start state, accepting too, with an ε-transition into the old start and ε-transitions back from the accepting states. r? means r + ε. Result: {{count}} states — det(·) turns it into a DFA.

unparseableCell.title: Unparseable cell
unparseableCell.detail: A cell is either a YAML definition (with a Machine / Grammar key) or an expression, optionally named: "name = expression".

duplicateDefinition.title: Duplicate definition: "{{name}}"
duplicateDefinition.detail: The name is defined by both cell {{other}} and cell {{index}} — the first definition wins; remove or rename the others.

circularDependency.title: Circular dependency
circularDependency.detail: The definition of "{{name}}" (indirectly) refers to itself: {{chain}}. Break the cycle.

brokenDependency.title: Broken dependency: {{missing}}
brokenDependency.detail: The referenced cell is broken or can't be evaluated yet — fix that one first.

machine.startNotInStates: The start state ({{start}}) is not among the states
machine.acceptNotInStates: The accepting state ({{state}}) is not among the states

badStoragesField.title: The storages field expects key-value pairs
badStoragesField.detail:
For example:
  storages:
    v1: stack
    v2:
      type: queue
      charset: A, B
      init: A

badInputField.title: The input field ({{input}}) is not the id of a storage
badInputField.detail: Use "head" (the read head), or the name of one of the storages: {{storages}}.

noAcceptSuggestEmptyStorages.title: No accepting state — for acceptance by empty storages, use acceptMode: emptyStorages
noAcceptSuggestEmptyStorages.detail: Without an accepting state and in finalState mode, the machine recognizes the empty language.

invalidTransition.title: Invalid transition: "{{line}}"
invalidTransition.detail: This machine's transitions read {{shape}}: δ's arguments in parentheses, an arrow, then its value, every part written out (ε too).

machine.unknownToState: Unknown target state in the transition: "{{state}}"

noAcceptState.title: No accepting state
noAcceptState.detail: The machine therefore recognizes the empty language.

nondeterministicMachine.title: Nondeterministic machine: more than one transition can match in state {{state}}
nondeterministicMachine.detail: The simulation follows every branch; click a highlighted edge on the graph to pick a specific branch.

storageCharsetNotOneSymbol.title: “{{symbol}}” in the alphabet of {{storageId}} is not one symbol
storageCharsetNotOneSymbol.detail: List the alphabet's symbols one by one, separated by commas. A symbol with a subscript is written with _, like {{example}}.

blankNotInTapeCharset.title: The blank _ is missing from the alphabet of {{storageId}}
blankNotInTapeCharset.detail: A tape holds blanks wherever nothing is written, so the blank is one of its symbols: _ ∈ Γ.

blankInInput.title: The blank _ cannot be an input symbol
blankInInput.detail: The input is written onto the tape {{storageId}}, where _ marks the empty cells: _ ∈ Γ \ Σ.

inputNotInStorageCharset.title: The alphabet of {{storageId}} lacks the input symbols {{symbols}}
inputNotInStorageCharset.detail: The input is written onto this storage, so every input symbol is one of its symbols too: Σ ⊆ Γ.

initNotInStorageCharset.title: The initial content of {{storageId}} uses “{{symbol}}”, which is not in its alphabet

unknownStorageSymbol.title: Unknown symbol “{{symbol}}” for {{storageId}}
unknownStorageSymbol.detail: Line: "{{line}}". The alphabet of {{storageId}} is Γ = {{gamma}} — any other symbol it may hold goes in its charset.

fieldHints.variables: The variables, e.g. variables: S, A, B
fieldHints.init: The start variable, e.g. init: S
fieldHints.charset: The terminals, e.g. charset: a, b
fieldHints.rules: The rules, e.g. rules: [S -> aA | b]

grammar.startNotInNonterminals: The start variable ({{start}}) is not among the variables

overlappingSymbols.title: Conflicting symbols: {{symbols}}
overlappingSymbols.detail: A symbol cannot be both a terminal and a variable.

emptyAlternative.title: Empty alternative in the rule: "{{line}}"
emptyAlternative.detail: Write ε (or eps) for the empty word, e.g. "S -> aS | ε".

invalidRule.title: Invalid rule: "{{line}}"
invalidRule.detail: Form: LEFT -> RIGHT1 | RIGHT2 — e.g. "S -> aA | b". Write ε (or eps) for the empty word.

grammar.unknownSymbolLeft: Unknown symbol on the left side of the rule: "{{symbol}}"
grammar.ruleDetail: Rule: "{{line}}". Every symbol must be listed in charset or variables.

leftMissingNonterminal.title: The left side of the rule contains no variable: "{{line}}"
leftMissingNonterminal.detail: In a generative grammar, the left side must contain at least one variable.

grammar.unknownSymbolRight: Unknown symbol on the right side of the rule: "{{symbol}}"

terminalNotOneChar.title: The terminal “{{symbol}}” is longer than one character
terminalNotOneChar.detail: Terminals are the characters of the words, so each is a single character. Variables may have subscripts: X_a, C_1.

ambiguousSubscript.title: “{{text}}” is ambiguous
ambiguousSubscript.detail: It could be the variable {{name}} or the symbols {{separate}}. Write {{name}} with _ for the variable, or separate the symbols with a space. ({{line}})

rangeTooLarge.title: Range too large in the {{field}} field: "{{range}}"

unknownStorageType.title: Unknown storage type for the "{{id}}" storage
unknownStorageType.detail:
Allowed: stack, queue, tape — with an alphabet and an initial content:
  v1:
    type: stack
    charset: Z, A
    init: Z

unknownMove.title: Unknown move: "{{tokens}}" ({{storageId}})
unknownMove.detail: Line: "{{line}}". Allowed: R (right), L (left), S (stay) — the YAML always uses these English letters, whatever the interface's language.

oneSymbol.title: “{{tokens}}” is more than one symbol ({{storageId}})
oneSymbol.detail: An operation takes a single symbol off the storage (or ε for nothing). A symbol with a subscript is written with _, like {{example}}. ({{line}})

tapeOneSymbol.title: “{{tokens}}” is not one tape symbol ({{storageId}})
tapeOneSymbol.detail: Line: "{{line}}". A tape cell always holds exactly one symbol — an empty one the blank _.

badName.title: “{{name}}” is not a name
badName.detail: A name is a single letter with an optional subscript — for example {{suggestion}}. Type _ to start the subscript; digits right after the letter go there by themselves (M1 is M₁).

infiniteOnlyForTape.title: Storage "{{id}}": infinite only applies to a tape
infiniteOnlyForTape.detail: A stack or a queue has no extent to choose — leave the infinite key out.

badInfinite.title: Storage "{{id}}": unknown tape extent "{{value}}"
badInfinite.detail: infinite: right — a tape infinite to the right from its first cell (the default); infinite: both — a tape infinite in both directions.

writableOnlyForTape.title: Storage "{{id}}": writable only applies to a tape
writableOnlyForTape.detail: A stack or a queue is always written — leave the writable key out.

badWritable.title: Storage "{{id}}": writable is true or false, not "{{value}}"
badWritable.detail: writable: true — the machine may write on the tape too; writable: false — it only reads it. By default the input tape of a machine with several storages is read-only (the machine works on its other storages); every other tape is writable.

needsDeterministic.title: The {{op}} operation requires a deterministic automaton
needsDeterministic.detail: Nondeterminism found: {{spots}}{{ellipsis}}. In a deterministic automaton every (state, symbol) pair has exactly one successor state and there is no ε-transition. The subset construction (determinization) builds an equivalent DFA, ε-transitions included.

needsComplete.title: The {{op}} operation requires a complete automaton
needsComplete.detail: Missing transitions: {{spots}}{{ellipsis}} — {{count}} (state, symbol) pairs have no transition defined in total. To complete it, we introduce a new "trap" (rejecting) state and route every missing transition there.

alreadyFree.title: The automaton is already ε-free
alreadyFree.detail: There is no ε-transition, so the operation returns the automaton unchanged.

step1.title: 1. Computing ε-closures
step1.detail: For every state q: E(q) = the set of states reachable from q using only ε-transitions (including q itself).

step2.title: 2. Introducing new transitions
step2.detail: δ'(q, a) = E(δ(E(q), a)) — transitions reachable through the ε-closure are made direct.

step3.title: 3. Extending the accepting states
step3.detailChanged: If E(q) contains an accepting state, q becomes accepting too. New accepting states: {{list}}.
step3.detailUnchanged: No state's ε-closure contains a new accepting state, so the accepting set is unchanged.

alreadyDeterministic.title: The automaton is already deterministic
alreadyDeterministic.detail: Every (state, symbol) pair has at most one transition and there is no ε-transition — the subset construction only creates the reachable one-element sets (and ∅ where a transition is missing).

step.title: Subset construction
step.detail: The new states are sets of the old ones; the start state is {{start}}. For every set R reached and every letter a: δ'(R, a) = ⋃ δ(r, a) over r ∈ R — where R has several elements, the parts are shown one by one. Only the sets reachable from the start are built, and a set accepts if it contains an accepting state.
step.detailEpsilon: The new states are sets of the old ones; the start state is {{startExpr}} = {{start}}. For every set R reached and every letter a: δ'(R, a) = ⋃ E(δ(r, a)) over r ∈ R — a letter is read, then any ε-transitions may follow. Where R has several elements, the parts E(δ(r, a)) are shown one by one. Only the sets reachable from the start are built, and a set accepts if it contains an accepting state.

result.title: Result
result.detail: {{count}} states were produced out of the possible 2^{{exponent}} = {{possible}} subsets. Accepting: {{accept}}.

closures.title: ε-closures
closures.detail: E(q) is the set of states reachable from q along ε-transitions — any number of them —, q included. The new automaton works with these closures: its start state is the closure of the start state, and after a letter it takes the closure of where the letter leads.

emptySet.title: The empty set ∅ appears — a trap state
emptySet.detail: Where a letter leads nowhere, δ'(R, a) = ∅: the empty set is a state too — it never accepts, and every letter keeps it there. So the result is a complete DFA.

anim.start: The start state is {{start}}. Each set stays dashed until its row is processed.
anim.startEpsilon: The start state is {{startExpr}} = {{start}}. Each set stays dashed until its row is processed.
anim.new: δ'({{set}}, {{symbol}}) = {{expr}} — a new set: it becomes a state, processed later.
anim.newAccept: δ'({{set}}, {{symbol}}) = {{expr}} — a new set: it becomes a state, accepting because it contains an accepting state.
anim.known: δ'({{set}}, {{symbol}}) = {{expr}} — this set is already a state: only the transition is new.
anim.empty: δ'({{set}}, {{symbol}}) = ∅ — no element has a {{symbol}}-transition: the empty set appears, the trap state.
anim.trap: ∅ goes to itself on every letter, and it is never accepting.
anim.done: Done: {{count}} states out of {{possible}} possible subsets — only those reachable from the start state were built.

alreadyComplete.title: The automaton is already complete
alreadyComplete.detail: Every (state, symbol) pair has a transition — nothing to do.

nameTaken.title: The state name "{{trap}}" already exists
nameTaken.detail: Completion needs a new, not-yet-used trap-state name.

step.title: Introducing the trap state: {{trap}}
step.detail: The new state {{trap}} is not accepting, and every symbol maps it to itself — once there, it can no longer accept. The missing transitions are routed here.

allReachable.title: Every state is reachable
allReachable.detail: Every state is reachable from the start state — there is nothing to drop.

step.title: Removing unreachable states
step.detail: The states reachable from the start state by a breadth-first traversal remain. Removed: {{removed}}.

unreachableStates.title: Unreachable states
unreachableStates.detail: No word leads from the start state into {{states}}. They have no place in the minimal automaton, so they go first — the result is the same as leaving them out at the end.

step1.title: Initial partition: 0-equivalence
step1.detail: A₁ = Q − F and A₂ = F: the empty word already tells the non-accepting and the accepting states apart. {{partition}}

refine.title: Round {{round}}: {{round}}-equivalence
refine.detail: Two states stay together when every letter takes them into the same group. Splitting: {{splits}}. New partition: {{partition}}. Now the states no word of length at most {{round}} tells apart are together ({{round}}-equivalence).

fixpoint.title: Round {{round}}: nothing splits
fixpoint.detail: In every group, every letter takes all states into the same group: {{round}}-equivalence is the same as {{prev}}-equivalence, and then no longer word tells the states apart either. The groups are the equivalence classes: {{partition}}.

alreadyMinimal.title: The automaton was already minimal
alreadyMinimal.detail: Every state ended up in its own equivalence class.

minimized.title: Minimized: {{before}} → {{after}} states
minimized.detail: States grouped into the same class are linguistically indistinguishable: they accept/reject every word the same way.

build.title: The new automaton from the classes
build.detail: Every class is a state. A letter takes all states of a class into the same class — that is the transition. The start state is the class of the old one, {{start}}; the accepting states are the classes of accepting states: {{accept}}.

anim.start: Initial partition (0-equivalence): {{partition}}. One colour is one group.
anim.split: End of round {{round}} — splits: {{splits}}. The new partition: {{partition}}.
anim.fixpoint: Round {{round}}: no group splits, the partition is final: {{partition}}.
anim.build: Each class becomes one state, in the colour of its class; the transitions run between the classes.

whyDfa.title: Why is a DFA required?
whyDfa.detail: For an NFA, flipping the accepting states does NOT yield the complement language: an NFA accepts a word if an accepting path EXISTS — after flipping, a rejecting path may still exist and become accepting too.

whyComplete.title: Why is completeness required?
whyComplete.detail: If a transition is missing somewhere, the automaton gets "stuck" and rejects. The complement should accept these words instead — this requires completing the automaton with a trap state first.

step.title: Flipping the accepting states
step.detail: In a complete DFA, every word runs along exactly one path, so swapping accepting/rejecting states yields exactly the complement language. New accepting set: {{accept}}.

hasEpsilon.title: The {{part}} automaton contains an ε-transition
hasEpsilon.detail: The product construction (running both in parallel) expects deterministic, complete automata, because the two automata must step in sync, symbol by symbol. An ε-transition would break this.

nondeterministic.title: The {{part}} automaton is nondeterministic
nondeterministic.detail: The states of the product automaton are (p, q) pairs, with δ((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a), δ₂(q,a)) — this requires both δ's to be single-valued.

incomplete.title: The {{part}} automaton is not complete
incomplete.detailUnion: If one automaton gets stuck, the pair can no longer step even though the other could still run — for a union, the other automaton's acceptance still matters. Completion (a trap state) fixes this.
incomplete.detailOther: If one automaton gets stuck, the pair can no longer step even though the other could still run — the result would be incorrect. Completion (a trap state) fixes this.

acceptRule.union: (p,q) is accepting if p OR q is accepting
acceptRule.intersect: (p,q) is accepting if p AND q are both accepting
acceptRule.difference: (p,q) is accepting if p is accepting but q is NOT (L₁ \ L₂)

step.title: Product construction ({{mode}})
step.detail: The two automata are run in parallel: the states are (p,q) pairs, δ((p,q),a) = (δ₁(p,a), δ₂(q,a)). Acceptance: {{acceptRule}}. Only reachable pairs are built.

extend.title: The {{part}} automaton over the common alphabet
extend.detail: {{name}} has no transition on {{missing}}: over Σ = {{sigma}} it is an incomplete automaton, so it is completed first — every missing transition leads into a new trap state {{trap}}, which never leaves. Its language does not change.

info.title: Union built via ε-construction
info.detail: An ε-transition leads from a new start state into both automata's start states. The result is an ε-NFA — det(·) turns it into a DFA. (A union of complete DFAs can also be done with the product construction.)

step.title: Union with ε-transitions
step.detail: New start state {{start}}, ε-transitions: {{start}} → {{m1start}}, {{start}} → {{bstart}}. Accepting states: the union of both automata's accepting states.

step.title: Concatenation
step.detail: An ε-transition leads from every accepting state of the first automaton to the second automaton's start state ({{start}}). Accepting: only the second automaton's accepting states. The result is an ε-NFA.

step.title: Kleene closure (star)
step.detail: New start state {{start}} (also accepting — so the empty word is in the language too), an ε-transition to the original start state, and from every accepting state an ε-transition back to {{start}} for repetition.

step.title: Reversal
step.detail: Every transition's direction is reversed, an ε-transition leads from the new start state ({{start}}) to the original accepting states, and the original start state becomes the sole accepting state. L(Mᴿ) = { wᴿ : w ∈ L(M) }.

numbering.title: Numbering the states
numbering.detail: The states are numbered 1…{{n}}; the start state {{start}} gets 1. r(p, q, t) describes the words that lead from state p to state q while every intermediate state is among 1…t.

base.title: r(p, q, 0) — no intermediate state
base.detail: The letters on the p → q edges, plus ε when p = q (and for an ε-edge); ∅ when there is nothing.

round.title: r(p, q, {{t}}) — passing through state {{state}} is allowed too
round.detail: r(p, q, {{t}}) = r(p, q, {{prev}}) + r(p, {{t}}, {{prev}}) r({{t}}, {{t}}, {{prev}})* r({{t}}, q, {{prev}}) — the word either avoids state {{t}}, or reaches it, returns to it any number of times and then leaves for q. Simplified with identities such as ∅ + r = r, r∅ = ∅, (a + ε)* = a*, (a + ε)a* = a* and b + a*b = a*b.

result.title: Result
result.detail: The language is the union of r(1, q, {{n}}) over the accepting states q: {{terms}} = {{regex}}
result.detailNone: There is no accepting state, so the language is empty: ∅.

tooLarge.title: The regular expression grows too large
tooLarge.detail: At step t = {{t}} (of {{n}}) an expression grew longer than {{limit}} characters. Minimize the automaton first — toRegex(min(…)) — for a much shorter expression.

multiCharSymbol.title: The symbol “{{symbol}}” is longer than one character
multiCharSymbol.detail: In a regular expression every letter is a single character, so every symbol of the alphabet must be one character long.

step.title: Renaming the states
step.detail: States get the names A, B, C… in the order they're visited starting from the start state. The language does not change.

counterexampleSearch.title: Searching for a counterexample in the product automaton
counterexampleSearch.detail: The two automata (made complete and deterministic) are run in parallel, searching for the shortest word accepted by exactly one of them. Found: "{{word}}".

proof.title: Proving equivalence
proof.detail: In every reachable (p,q) state pair of the product automaton, p and q's acceptance status agree, so there is no distinguishing word — the two automata recognize the same language.

det.title: Determinizing {{name}}
det.detail: {{name}} is not a complete deterministic automaton, so the subset construction turns it into a complete DFA: {{count}} states.

extend.title: {{name}} over the common alphabet
extend.detail: {{name}} has no transition on {{missing}}: those letters lead into a new trap state {{trap}}, so the alphabet is common and the language stays the same.

search.title: Looking for a distinguishing word in the product automaton
search.detailFound: L({{a}}) = L({{b}}) exactly when (L({{a}}) ∩ ¬L({{b}})) ∪ (¬L({{a}}) ∩ L({{b}})) = ∅. The two automata run side by side (the product automaton), and a breadth-first search looks for the first reachable pair (p, q) where exactly one accepts. The table shows the pairs in the order of the search, up to the one found.
search.detailNone: L({{a}}) = L({{b}}) exactly when (L({{a}}) ∩ ¬L({{b}})) ∪ (¬L({{a}}) ∩ L({{b}})) = ∅. The two automata run side by side (the product automaton): in all {{count}} reachable pairs (p, q) both accept or both reject, so the language of the difference is empty.

needsContextFree.title: This operation ({{op}}) needs rules of the form A → α
needsContextFree.detail: Every rule's left-hand side must be a single variable — ε-rules are fine. The Chomsky classification panel shows which rule breaks this.

classify.startEpsilonNotAllowed: {{start}} → ε is only allowed if {{start}} occurs on no right-hand side — but it does here
classify.deletingRule: {{rule}} is an ε-rule (ε is only allowed as S → ε)
classify.epsilonNotOnStart: {{rule}} — an ε-rule not on the start variable
classify.startOnRightWithEpsilon: alongside {{start}} → ε, {{start}} also occurs on a right-hand side — so the grammar is not in ε-free form
classify.notRegularRule: rule {{rule}} is not of the form A → aB or A → a
classify.leftNotSingleVariable: the left side of rule {{rule}} is not a single variable
classify.notContextSensitive: rule {{rule}} is not of the form βAγ → βαγ (a variable A replaced in place by a nonempty α)

needsRightLinear.title: Only a right-linear grammar can be turned into a finite automaton
needsRightLinear.detail: Every rule must be A → aB or A → a (type 3), or more generally A → uB, A → u, A → B or A → ε with a terminal word u. The construction: every variable becomes a state; A → aB becomes the transition A →a B; A → a a transition into a new accepting state E; A → ε makes A accepting.

step.title: Right-linear grammar → NFA
step.detail: Every variable becomes a state, the start variable is the start state, and a new state {{end}} is the accepting one. From A → aB: an a-transition from A to B; from A → a: an a-transition into {{end}}; with S → ε, S accepts too. A longer word u in A → uB or A → u gets new states in between, A → B becomes an ε-transition and A → ε makes A accepting.

renamed.title: Some states got A_q variable names

step.title: Variables for the states
step.detail: Every state q gets a variable A_q — the state's own name when it already is a valid variable name. The start state's variable is the start variable.

needsEpsilonFree.title: An automaton without ε-transitions is needed for a grammar
needsEpsilonFree.detail: The construction turns a transition δ(q, a) = p into A_q → aA_p — an ε-transition ({{list}}) would give a rule A_q → A_p, which no type-3 grammar has. Remove the ε-transitions first.

newStart.title: A start state with no incoming transition
newStart.detail: {{start}} accepts, so the grammar gets S → ε — and then S may occur on no right-hand side. But transitions lead into {{start}}: a new state {{copy}}, a copy of {{start}} (accepting as well), takes them over and moves on just as {{start}} does. The language stays the same.

rules.title: Rules from the transitions
rules.detail: δ(q, a) = p gives A_q → aA_p: after reading a, the derivation goes on from p. When p accepts, A_q → a as well: the word may end there. When the start state accepts, S → ε. Every rule is A → aB or A → a, and S → ε comes only with S on no right-hand side: the grammar is type 3 and generates the automaton's language.

needsContextFree.title: Only a grammar of A → α rules can be turned into a pushdown automaton
needsContextFree.detail: In the construction the stack holds the rest of the sentential form, and a variable on its top is replaced by a right-hand side — so every left-hand side must be a single variable. The Chomsky classification panel shows which rule breaks this.

emptyStackInfo.title: Built a PDA that accepts by empty stack
emptyStackInfo.detail: The stack holds the derivation's current sentential form. If a variable is on top of the stack, a rule is applied (an ε-step); if a terminal, it's matched against the next input letter. A word is accepted exactly when the input is exhausted and the stack is empty.

step.title: CF grammar → pushdown automaton
step.detail: A single state {{q}}; the stack starts with {{z0}}. First (q, ε, {{z0}}) → (q, {{start}}{{z1}}): the start variable goes onto the stack, {{z1}} below it. A variable on top: for every rule A → α, (q, ε, A) → (q, α) — {{ruleCount}} such steps. A terminal on top: (q, a, a) → (q, ε) matches it with the next input letter — {{terminalCount}} such steps. Finally (q, ε, {{z1}}) → (q, ε): when the sentential form is used up, the stack empties, and the word is accepted with an empty stack.

needsContextFree.title: ε-removal works on grammars of A → α rules
needsContextFree.detail: Removing the ε-rules leaves variables out of right-hand sides, so every left-hand side must be a single variable. The Chomsky classification panel shows which rule breaks this.

step1.title: 1. Nullable variables
step1.detailNone: No nullable variable — the grammar is already ε-free.
step1.detailSome: N₁ holds the variables with an ε-rule; N(i+1) adds every A that has a rule A → α where every symbol of α is already in N(i). It stops when a round adds nothing. Nullable (derivable to ε): {{nullable}}.

step2.title: 2. Extending the rules
step2.detail: Every rule is replaced by all of its variants in which some of the nullable variables are dropped — except the empty right-hand side and the useless A → A. The ε-rules themselves are discarded.

step3.title: 3. New start variable because of ε
step3.detail: The original language contains ε (the start variable is nullable), so we introduce a new start variable {{s2}}: {{s2}} → {{start}} | ε. This way the ε-rule remains only on the start variable.

step1.title: 1. The graph of unit rules
step1.detail: Unit rules (A → B): {{edges}}. U(A) is the set of variables reachable from A along them, A included.
step1.detailNone: There is no unit rule (A → B) — the grammar stays the same.

step2.title: 2. New rules
step2.detail: The unit rules are dropped, and every A gets the other rules B → β of each B ∈ U(A) as A → β.

epsilonFirst.title: The grammar still has ε-rules
epsilonFirst.detail: Removing the ε-rules afterwards can create new unit rules (A → BC with a nullable C gives A → B), so the ε-rules are removed first.

step1.title: 1. Variables that derive a terminal word
step1.detail: B₀ = Σ, and Bᵢ₊₁ adds every A with a rule A → α whose symbols are all in Bᵢ. The variables outside the final set derive no terminal word; their rules are dropped: {{removed}}.
step1.detailNone: B₀ = Σ, and Bᵢ₊₁ adds every A with a rule A → α whose symbols are all in Bᵢ. Every variable derives a terminal word.

step2.title: 2. Symbols reachable from the start variable
step2.detail: T₀ = {S}, and Tᵢ₊₁ adds every symbol on the right-hand side of a rule of a variable in Tᵢ. Unreachable, dropped: {{removed}}.
step2.detailNone: T₀ = {S}, and Tᵢ₊₁ adds every symbol on the right-hand side of a rule of a variable in Tᵢ. Every remaining symbol is reachable.

emptyLanguage.title: The language is empty
emptyLanguage.detail: The start variable {{start}} derives no terminal word, so L(G) = ∅ — every rule is useless.

needsEpsilonFree.title: The Chomsky normal form needs an ε-free grammar
needsEpsilonFree.detail: The construction assumes that ε occurs only as S → ε with S on no right-hand side; remove the ε-rules first.

epsilonDropped.title: ε is left out
epsilonDropped.detail: A grammar in Chomsky normal form cannot generate ε, so the rule {{start}} → ε is dropped: the result generates L(G) \ {ε}.

step2.title: Dropping the ε-rule
step2.detail: The rule {{start}} → ε is dropped: there is no ε-rule in Chomsky normal form.

step3.title: Variables for the terminals
step3.detail: In every right-hand side of length at least 2, a terminal a is replaced by a new variable X_a with the rule X_a → a.

step4.title: Breaking the long rules
step4.detail: A → B₁B₂…Bₖ (k > 2) becomes A → B₁C₁, C₁ → B₂C₂, …, Cₖ₋₂ → Bₖ₋₁Bₖ with new variables Cᵢ.

already.title: Already in Chomsky normal form
already.detail: Every rule is A → a or A → BC.

needsCNF.title: CYK needs a grammar in Chomsky normal form
needsCNF.detail: Every rule must be A → a or A → BC.

needsPda.title: {{op}} needs a pushdown automaton
needsPda.detail: This construction works on a machine with an input head and a single stack. A machine without storage is a finite automaton: toGrammar gives its regular grammar.

step.title: Acceptance by final state → by empty stack
step.detail: A new start state {{start}} puts a new symbol {{z}} at the bottom of the stack, under its start content: {{first}}. M never takes {{z}} out, so the stack cannot empty while M runs — not even where M's own stack would. From every accepting state ({{accept}}) the machine may go to {{qe}}, taking any symbol, and {{qe}} empties the stack: a word is accepted by empty stack exactly when M reaches an accepting state with the word read.

already.title: The pushdown automaton already accepts by empty stack
already.detail: Nothing to convert: the result is the machine itself.

step.title: Acceptance by empty stack → by final state
step.detail: A new start state {{start}} puts a new symbol {{z}} at the bottom of the stack, under its start content: {{first}}. M′ never takes {{z}} out, so when only {{z}} is left, M′ has emptied its stack — then from any of its states the machine goes to {{qf}}, the only accepting state, where it stops: (q, ε, {{z}}) → ({{qf}}, {{z}}).

already.title: The pushdown automaton already accepts by final state
already.detail: Nothing to convert: the result is the machine itself.

bottom.title: A bottom symbol for the stack first
bottom.detailInit: The stack starts with {{init}}, not with a single symbol Z₀ as the construction needs. A new start state {{start}} writes it above a new bottom symbol {{z}}: {{first}}. Only (q, ε, {{z}}) → ({{qe}}, ε) takes {{z}} out, into {{qe}}, where nothing moves — so the stack is empty only at the end, and the machine accepts by empty stack the same words.
bottom.detailEmptied: The construction's first step lets a transition that takes nothing from the stack take every symbol and put it back. That keeps the language only when the machine cannot move once its stack is empty — but here the stack can empty in {{state}}, and {{transition}} still moves from there. So first a new bottom symbol {{z}} goes under the stack's content: {{first}}. Only (q, ε, {{z}}) → ({{qe}}, ε) takes {{z}} out, into {{qe}}, where nothing moves — so the stack is empty only at the end, and the machine accepts by empty stack the same words.

replace.title: 1. Every step takes a symbol from the stack
replace.detail: (q′, α) ∈ δ(q, a, ε) is replaced by (q′, αA) ∈ δ(q, a, A) for every A ∈ Γ: the symbol on top is taken and put back. The variables [qAp] need this — every step takes exactly one symbol from the stack.
replace.detailNone: Every transition takes a symbol from the stack already: nothing to replace.

variables.title: 2. The variables [qAp]
variables.detail: V = {[qAp] : q, p ∈ Q, A ∈ Γ} ∪ {S}: {{states}}² · {{symbols}} + 1 = {{count}} variables. [qAp] stands for A put on the stack in state q and taken out — with everything that came in its place — in state p: it derives exactly the words x with (q, x, A) ⇒* (p, ε, ε); {{example}} for instance. S is the start variable: {{startRules}}, as a word is accepted when the machine, started in {{q0}} with {{z0}}, empties its stack in some state.

rules.title: 3. Rules from the transitions
rules.detail: (q′, ε) ∈ δ(q, a, A) gives [qAq′] → a; (q′, B₁…B_k) ∈ δ(q, a, A) gives [qAq″] → a[q′B₁q₂][q₂B₂q₃]…[q_kB_kq″] for every choice of the states q₂, …, q_k, q″ — |Q|^k rules. With a = ε a rule can be [qAq′] → ε: every rule is A → α, and after ε-removal the grammar is of class 2. {{count}} rules in all.

tooLarge.title: The grammar would have {{count}} rules
tooLarge.detail: A transition writing k symbols gives |Q|^k rules. Beyond {{max}} rules the grammar is not built — a machine with fewer states or shorter words written on the stack gives a smaller one.

badLabel.title: Some names cannot stand in a variable [qAp]
badLabel.detail: {{labels}}: the states and stack symbols are written inside the variables, so they may hold no space, bracket, comma, backslash or |. Rename them.

ambiguousNames.title: Two variables would both be {{name}}
ambiguousNames.detail: The state, symbol, state triples {{a}} and {{b}} written side by side give the same text. Rename a state, so that every [qAp] is different.

useless.title: {{useless}} of the {{count}} variables are useless
useless.detail: The construction makes [qAp] for every two states and every symbol, also where the machine can never take A out in p after putting it on in q. The grammar is right as it is; removing the useless symbols (trim) leaves the same language with far fewer rules.

search.title: Can an accepting state be reached from the start state?
search.detailFound: L = ∅ exactly when no path leads from the start state to an accepting state. A breadth-first search from the start state; an ε-transition reads no letter, so those are followed first, and every state is reached by a shortest word leading there. The accepting state {{state}} is reachable: the language is not empty, and {{word}} is a shortest word of it.
search.detailNone: L = ∅ exactly when no path leads from the start state to an accepting state. The breadth-first search from the start state reaches {{count}} states, none of them accepting — the automaton accepts no word, L = ∅.

search.title: Looking for a common word in the product automaton
search.detailFound: Whether L₁ ∩ L₂ = ∅ is the emptiness of the intersection. The states of its automaton are the pairs (p, q): a letter moves both automata, an ε-transition only its own. Only the pairs reachable from the start pair are built, breadth-first, each with a shortest word leading there. In the pair {{pair}} both states accept: {{word}} is in both languages, so they are not disjoint.
search.detailNone: Whether L₁ ∩ L₂ = ∅ is the emptiness of the intersection. The states of its automaton are the pairs (p, q): a letter moves both automata, an ε-transition only its own. {{count}} pairs are reachable from the start pair, and in none of them do both states accept: the intersection is empty, the languages are disjoint.

min.title: The minimal automaton
min.detMin: The language is infinite exactly when it has a word w with n ≤ |w| ≤ 2n, n the number of states of its minimal automaton. The automaton determinized and minimized: n = {{n}} states.
min.completeMin: The language is infinite exactly when it has a word w with n ≤ |w| ≤ 2n, n the number of states of its minimal automaton. The automaton completed and minimized: n = {{n}} states.
min.min: The language is infinite exactly when it has a word w with n ≤ |w| ≤ 2n, n the number of states of its minimal automaton. The automaton minimized: n = {{n}} states.

lengths.title: Is there a word with a length between n and 2n?
lengths.detailFound: The words need not be followed one by one: Rₖ is the set of states some word of length k leads to (R₀ = {q₀}, Rₖ₊₁ = δ(Rₖ, Σ)), and the language has a word of length k exactly when Rₖ ∩ F ≠ ∅. The first such length between n = {{n}} and 2n = {{twoN}} is k = {{k}}: {{word}} is a shortest word of the language at least n long — the language is infinite.
lengths.detailNone: The words need not be followed one by one: Rₖ is the set of states some word of length k leads to (R₀ = {q₀}, Rₖ₊₁ = δ(Rₖ, Σ)), and the language has a word of length k exactly when Rₖ ∩ F ≠ ∅. For no k with n = {{n}} ≤ k ≤ 2n = {{twoN}} does Rₖ contain an accepting state: the language has no word with a length between n and 2n, so it is finite.

pump.title: Pumping the word
pump.detail: Reading {{word}}, the state {{state}} repeats within the first n letters, so the word splits as x = uvw: u = {{u}}, v = {{v}}, w = {{w}}, with |uv| ≤ n and |v| ≥ 1. v leads from {{state}} back to {{state}}, so it can be repeated any number of times: uvᵏw ∈ L for every k ≥ 0 — {{words}}, … Infinitely many words.

words.title: The words of the language
words.detail: Every word of a finite language is shorter than n = {{n}} (a word at least n long could be pumped). The language has {{count}} words.
words.detailEmpty: The language has no word at all: L = ∅, so it is finite.

emptyGrammar.title: Does the start variable derive a terminal word?
emptyGrammar.detailFound: L(G) = ∅ exactly when the start variable is useless: it derives no terminal word. B₀ = Σ, and Bᵢ₊₁ adds every A with a rule A → α whose symbols are all in Bᵢ. The start variable {{start}} enters in round {{round}}: the language is not empty, and {{word}} is a shortest word of it.
emptyGrammar.detailNone: L(G) = ∅ exactly when the start variable is useless: it derives no terminal word. B₀ = Σ, and Bᵢ₊₁ adds every A with a rule A → α whose symbols are all in Bᵢ. The start variable {{start}} never enters: it derives no terminal word, the language is empty.

prepare.title: Preparation: ε-rules, unit rules and useless symbols removed
prepare.detail: The language is infinite exactly when it has a word w with p ≤ |w| ≤ 2p, p the pumping length. Such a word has a derivation tree with a path on which a variable repeats — the proof of the pumping lemma shows this on a grammar with no unit rules and no ε-rule other than S → ε; with the useless symbols removed too, every variable takes part in deriving some word. Such a grammar for the same language:
prepare.detailEmpty: The start variable derives no terminal word: the language is empty, so it is finite.

repeat.title: Can a variable repeat in a derivation tree?
repeat.detailFound: A variable can repeat on a path of a derivation tree exactly when it derives a sentential form containing itself: A ⇒⁺ …A…. For every variable A the table gives the variables on the right-hand sides of its rules, and the variables B with A ⇒⁺ …B…. Variables leading back to themselves: {{variables}} — the language is infinite.
repeat.detailNone: A variable can repeat on a path of a derivation tree exactly when it derives a sentential form containing itself: A ⇒⁺ …A…. For every variable A the table gives the variables on the right-hand sides of its rules, and the variables B with A ⇒⁺ …B…. No variable derives a sentential form containing itself: no variable repeats on any path of any derivation tree, so the trees are bounded (at most {{m}} variables on a path), and the language is finite.

pump.title: Pumping the word
pump.detail: {{start}} ⇒* {{outer}} and {{variable}} ⇒⁺ {{inner}}; writing a shortest word of each variable in its place gives z = uvwxy with u = {{u}}, v = {{v}}, w = {{w}}, x = {{x}}, y = {{y}} (w a shortest word of {{variable}}). The step {{variable}} ⇒⁺ v{{variable}}x can be repeated any number of times, and as there are no unit rules and no ε-rules, |vx| ≥ 1: uvᵏwxᵏy ∈ L for every k ≥ 0 — {{words}}, … Infinitely many words.

words.title: The words of the language
words.detail: As no variable can repeat, the words of the variables can be computed bottom-up: first for those whose rules contain no variable, then for those that use only these. The language has {{count}} words.
words.detailCapped: As no variable can repeat, the words of the variables can be computed bottom-up: first for those whose rules contain no variable, then for those that use only these. The language has at least {{count}} words — no more are listed.

error.missingCloseParenRegex: Missing closing parenthesis in the regex() call (position {{pos}})
error.missingCommaOrParen: Missing "," or ")" in the function call (position {{pos}})
error.functionNeedsParen: The function name "{{word}}" must be followed by parentheses (position {{pos}})
error.unknownName: Unknown name: "{{word}}" — refer to machines by their name; a letter sequence can only be used inside regex(…) (position {{pos}})

wrongArgCount.exact: The function {{fn}} expects {{n}} argument(s), but {{count}} were given
wrongArgCount.range: The function {{fn}} expects {{n}} or {{alsoOk}} arguments, but {{count}} were given

error.needsFsm: {{ctx}}: expects a finite automaton, but got {{kind}}
error.machineNeedsFsm: {{ctx}}: expects a finite automaton, but {{name}} is {{machineKind}} (storages: {{storages}}). The language recognized by a machine with storage is generally not regular, so there is no automatic conversion — automaton operations only apply to storage-free machines.
error.machineHasStorage: {{name}} cannot be converted to a finite automaton because it has storage ({{storages}}) — only a storage-free machine has an equivalent automaton
error.undecidableMachine: {{op}}: {{name}} is a {{machineKind}}, and for the languages of such machines the question cannot be decided by an algorithm in general. For regular and context-free languages it can: a finite automaton, a regular expression, a pushdown automaton, a type-2 or type-3 grammar.
error.undecidableGrammar: {{op}}: not every rule of {{name}} is of the form A → α — for a type-0 or type-1 grammar the question cannot be decided by an algorithm in general; for regular and context-free languages it can.
error.toFsmExpects: toFsm() expects a grammar, a regular expression, or a storage-free machine
error.needsPda: {{op}}: expects a pushdown automaton, but got {{kind}}
error.parseGeneric: {{message}}. Examples: D = det(M) · U = union(M_1, M_2) · R = regex((ab)*+ba) · E = equal(M_1, M_2)
error.multiLetterName: “{{word}}” is not a name: a name is a single letter with an optional subscript, like {{suggestion}} (position {{pos}})

eval.literalsOnlyInRegex: Letter literals can only be used inside regex(…)

regex.title: Automatically converted the regex {{name}} to an ε-NFA
regex.detail: The operation expects a finite automaton; one is built from the regular expression — explicitly: toFsm({{name}}).

grammar.title: Automatically converted the grammar {{name}} to a finite automaton
grammar.detail: The operation expects a finite automaton; the right-linear grammar can be converted.

regexNameInside.title: {{names}} in regex(…) is just letters
regexNameInside.detail: A regular expression can't refer to other definitions — here {{name}} means the letters {{letters}}. To combine it with the definition {{name}}, do it outside the regex, e.g. {{name}} + regex(…) or union({{name}}, …). For the regular expression of the automaton {{name}}, use toRegex({{name}}).

det.summary: A deterministic automaton whose states are sets of states of {{a}}: a state holds every state {{a}} can be in after the letters read so far.
det.input: {{a}}: a finite automaton — nondeterministic too, with ε-transitions too
det.output: a complete deterministic finite automaton; only the sets reachable from the start are made

min.summary: States that no word tells apart are merged, so the language is accepted with as few states as possible.
min.output: a complete deterministic finite automaton with the fewest states, unique up to the names of its states
min.guarantee: L({{op}}) = L({{a}}), and no complete deterministic automaton of fewer states accepts it

fsm.summary: The ε-transitions go: a letter moves wherever it could move together with ε-transitions before and after it.
fsm.output: a finite automaton with the same states and no ε-transition — nondeterministic in general

grammar.summary: The ε-rules go: every rule also gets its variants without the variables that can derive ε.
grammar.input: {{a}}: a context-free grammar (every rule of the form A → α)
grammar.output: an ε-free grammar: no ε-rule, except that a new start variable, on no right-hand side, derives ε when ε is in the language

complete.summary: Every missing transition leads into a new trap state, which no word leaves again.
complete.output: a finite automaton with a transition from every state on every letter

reachable.summary: The states that no word leads to from the start state are dropped.
reachable.output: the part of {{a}} reachable from its start state

complement.summary: The accepting and the rejecting states swap roles.
complement.input: {{a}}: a complete deterministic finite automaton over the alphabet Σ
complement.output: a complete deterministic finite automaton with the same states and transitions

product.summary: The two automata run side by side: a state is a pair of their states, and a pair accepts when either part does.
product.input: {{a}}, {{b}}: complete deterministic finite automata — over different alphabets, each is completed over the common one
product.output: a complete deterministic finite automaton on the pairs of states

epsilon.summary: A new start state leads by ε-transitions to both start states: a word may follow a path of either automaton.
epsilon.output: a nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-transitions that contains both

intersect.summary: The two automata run side by side: a state is a pair of their states, and a pair accepts when both parts do.
intersect.input: {{a}}, {{b}}: complete deterministic finite automata — over different alphabets, each is completed over the common one
intersect.output: a complete deterministic finite automaton on the pairs of states

difference.summary: The two automata run side by side: a state is a pair of their states, and a pair accepts when the first part accepts and the second does not.
difference.input: {{a}}, {{b}}: complete deterministic finite automata — over different alphabets, each is completed over the common one
difference.output: a complete deterministic finite automaton on the pairs of states

concat.summary: An ε-transition leads from every accepting state of {{a}} to the start state of {{b}}: a word is read first by {{a}}, then by {{b}}.
concat.output: a nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-transitions; its accepting states are those of {{b}}

star.summary: A new start state, itself accepting, leads by ε into {{a}}, and the accepting states of {{a}} lead back to it: any number of words of the language, one after the other, are read.
star.output: a nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-transitions

reverse.summary: Every transition turns around; a new start state leads by ε to the accepting states, and the old start state is the only accepting one.
reverse.output: a nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-transitions

clean.summary: The states are renamed A, B, C, … in breadth-first order from the start state.
clean.output: the same automaton with new state names

fsm.summary: Every state becomes a variable, and a transition from q to p on a becomes the rule A_q → aA_p.

pda.summary: The variable [qAp] derives exactly the words that take the machine from state q to state p while A leaves the stack.
pda.input: {{a}}: a pushdown automaton, accepting by final state or by empty stack

regex.summary: An automaton for every part of the expression, from the letters up, joined as its operators say.
regex.output: a nondeterministic finite automaton with ε-transitions

grammar.summary: Every variable becomes a state, and the rule A → aB becomes a transition from A to B on a; A → a leads into a new accepting state.

toRegex.summary: The states are numbered, and r(p, q, t) — the words leading from p to q through states numbered at most t — is built for t = 0, 1, 2, …

toPda.summary: A machine of one state carries out a leftmost derivation on its stack: a variable on top is replaced by a right-hand side of it, a letter on top is matched with the input.
toPda.output: a pushdown automaton accepting by empty stack

unitfree.summary: A variable A takes over the other rules of every variable it reaches through rules A → B, and those rules go.
unitfree.output: a grammar without rules of the form A → B

trim.summary: First the variables that derive no terminal word go, then the symbols the start variable cannot reach.
trim.output: a grammar in which every symbol takes part in deriving some word

cnf.summary: Unit rules out, the letters of long right-hand sides replaced by new variables X_a → a, and right-hand sides longer than two cut into a chain of new variables.
cnf.output: a grammar in Chomsky normal form: every rule is A → BC or A → a

toEmptyStack.summary: In an accepting state the machine may empty its stack; a new bottom symbol keeps the stack from emptying any earlier.
toEmptyStack.input: {{a}}: a pushdown automaton accepting by final state
toEmptyStack.output: a pushdown automaton accepting by empty stack

toFinalState.summary: A new bottom symbol shows when the stack of {{a}} would be empty: then the machine moves into a new accepting state.
toFinalState.input: {{a}}: a pushdown automaton accepting by empty stack
toFinalState.output: a pushdown automaton accepting by final state

equal.summary: A breadth-first search over the pairs of states of the two automata looks for a word that exactly one of them accepts.
equal.output: yes or no — when no, with a shortest word that tells them apart

empty.summary: A word of the language is looked for: a path from the start state to an accepting state, or a terminal word the start variable derives.
empty.input: {{a}}: a finite automaton, a regular expression, a context-free grammar or a pushdown automaton
empty.output: yes or no — when no, with a shortest word of the language

finite.summary: The language is infinite exactly when one of its words can be pumped: a state repeats while it is read, or a variable derives itself again.
finite.input: {{a}}: a finite automaton, a regular expression, a context-free grammar or a pushdown automaton
finite.output: yes or no — when yes, the words of the language; when no, a word that can be pumped
finite.guarantee: yes exactly when L({{a}}) is finite

disjoint.summary: The two automata run side by side, and a word both of them accept is looked for.
disjoint.output: yes or no — when no, with a shortest word of both languages
